title: Hash Map
body:
[[Hashing]]
[[Hash Function]]
[[Prime Number]]

The structure that implements [[Maps]] using [[Hashing]]: an [[Array]] of slots, plus a
[[Hash Function]] that computes which slot a key belongs in. `get` and `put` hash the key
and go straight there, so both are $O(1)$ on average. No comparisons, no traversal, no
search.

```java
Map<String, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
counts.put("apple", 3);
counts.put("pear", 7);
counts.get("apple");        // 3, one hash and one index
```

## What you are buying and paying

| | |
|---|---|
| Lookup, insert, delete | $O(1)$ average, $O(n)$ worst |
| Space | $O(n)$, plus the empty slots the load factor demands |
| Ordering | none |

The worst case needs every key to collide, which takes a bad [[Hash Function]] or
deliberately chosen keys. The real everyday cost is the other row: **no ordering**. A hash
map cannot give you sorted output, a range of keys, or the next key after a given one,
because the hash deliberately scatters them. Iterating one gives an order that is arbitrary
and may change when the table resizes.

When order matters, use a [[Balanced Tree]] instead and accept $O(\log n)$. In [[Java]] that
is the `HashMap` versus `TreeMap` choice, both behind the same `Map` interface.

## Practical notes

- Keep the **load factor** (entries over slots) below about 0.7. Past that the table
  rehashes into a larger array, which is $O(n)$ but amortises away.
- Table size is usually a [[Prime Number]], so modulo mixes the whole hash value rather than
  keeping only the low bits.
- A key used in a hash map must have a stable hash. Mutating a key after inserting it puts
  the entry in a slot the lookup will never check, and the entry is effectively lost. In
  Java that also means `equals` and `hashCode` must agree: equal objects must hash equally,
  or the map will store duplicates it cannot find.

## Related

- Not to be confused with [[Hash Map Pattern]], the interview note in `Leetcode/`. This note
  is the structure; that one is the habit of reaching for it (complements, duplicates,
  frequencies, prefix-state counts).
